title: Universal constructions, quotients and equivalence
central_question: Which maps descend through a quotient, and which reversible constructions preserve the whole mathematical problem?
synopsis:
The categorical thread becomes strongest when a named operation is replaced by a construction with a testable mapping property. A quotient first declares which distinctions are erased. A pushout identifies two copies of shared data. An adjunction converts one kind of mapping problem into another, while an equivalence supplies inverse functors and natural comparison maps. These statements organize mathematics across the archive because they separate an object from a chosen presentation and make compatibility part of the theorem. They also distinguish several levels of preservation: agreement of dimensions is weaker than an isomorphism, an isomorphism of individual objects is weaker than a natural equivalence, and an equivalence of categories must respect the specified morphisms.

The useful starting point is the category of linear dynamical systems. An object is a vector space with an endomorphism A; a morphism L satisfies LA=BL. This single equation guarantees L exp(tA)=exp(tB)L by the power series, so composition preserves dynamics rather than merely relabeling coordinates. The tensor–Hom correspondence then makes composition of structures explicit. Currying is available for arbitrary algebraic vector spaces, whereas a duality datum with coevaluation requires finite dimension. This distinction prevents an infinite formal basis sum from being treated as an algebraic tensor. Reconstruction has a similar demand: a finite group can be recovered from the natural automorphisms of the forgetful functor on all finite G-sets, using the regular G-set and its equivariant maps; one representation or one dimension table cannot carry the same information.
definitions: For linear maps i:A→B and j:A→C, their pushout is P=(B⊕C)/R with R={(i(a),−j(a)):a∈A}. The structure maps send b and c to their corresponding quotient classes.

A categorical equivalence consists of functors F and G with natural isomorphisms GF≅Id and FG≅Id. An adjunction instead supplies natural bijections of Hom sets, with unit and counit satisfying the triangle identities.
In algebraic vector spaces, a duality datum ev:W⊗V→k and coev:k→V⊗W must reconstruct every vector through both triangle identities. Every algebraic tensor is a finite sum.

theorem.statement: The stated P is a pushout of i and j. Its dimension is dimB+dimC−rank(a↦(i(a),−j(a))). In particular the subtraction is dimA when at least one of i or j is injective. A vector space is dualizable under algebraic tensor product exactly when it is finite dimensional.
theorem.proof: Given compatible maps u:B→V and v:C→V with ui=vj, the map (b,c)↦u(b)+v(c) kills every (i(a),−j(a)). It therefore descends uniquely to P because the quotient map is surjective. Conversely every map from P gives such a compatible pair by composition. Rank-nullity gives the dimension formula, including the correction needed when both legs have a common kernel. For finite-dimensional V choose a basis e_r and its dual basis; coev(1)=Σe_r⊗e^r and evaluation give v=Σe^r(v)e_r. Conversely, if coev(1)=Σ_{r=1}^n v_r⊗w_r, one triangle identity writes every v as Σv_r ev(w_r⊗v). Thus finitely many v_r span V. This proves the finite-dimensional necessity directly, rather than inferring duality from an informal adjunction symbol.

worked_example.setup: Take A=Q, B=C=Q², i(a)=(a,0), j(a)=(0,a). Let u(b₁,b₂)=b₁+2b₂ and v(c₁,c₂)=3c₁+c₂.
worked_example.calculation: The relation is (a,0,0,−a), so P has dimension three. Coordinates (b₁+c₂,b₂,c₁) are invariant under this relation and identify P with Q³. The compatible functional descends to w(x,y,z)=x+2y+3z. For b=(2,1), c=(3,4), w(6,1,3)=17=u(b)+v(c). The equality is a certificate for this mapping problem, not just a matching dimension count.
worked_example.meaning: Universal properties are practical interfaces: later calculations can use the descended map without choosing representatives. Quotienting is information loss with a declared kernel, while equivalence preserves the specified category. Neither operation automatically supplies a metric, topology, probability model or computationally efficient algorithm.

title: Chain complexes, exactness and certificates of equivalence
central_question: How can a reduction preserve homology, and what finite identities certify that nothing essential was lost?
synopsis:
A chain complex records permitted boundaries and the relations among them. Its defining equation d²=0 is the first useful certificate: every boundary is a cycle, so a quotient of cycles by boundaries exists. The archive repeatedly approaches more elaborate constructions through this same requirement. Total complexes need Koszul signs; mapping cones need a genuine chain map; a blocked representation needs maps and a chain homotopy before it can inherit the original cohomology. These are constructive conditions. They provide explicit witnesses that a smaller calculation preserves the invariant instead of only producing similar output on an example.

The key distinction is between changing a presentation and changing an object. Adding a contractible pair increases the number of coordinates while preserving homology. Consequently total chain dimension cannot define an invariant of the derived object. Conversely a cochain map can annihilate a nonzero class, so the fact that an operation is linear or functorial does not prove that it preserves obstruction spaces. The finite Hodge decomposition gives a third view: with declared positive inner products, harmonic vectors represent homology, but that representative depends on the metric while the quotient space is invariant under chain equivalence. The supertrace index then becomes an exact cancellation statement, because all nonzero differential modes occur in paired even and odd degrees. No asymptotic heat approximation is required in the finite model.
definitions: A cochain complex has d:Cⁿ→Cⁿ⁺¹ with d²=0 and Hⁿ=ker dⁿ/im dⁿ⁻¹. A cochain map f satisfies d_D f=f d_C.
A contraction onto H consists of maps i:H→C, p:C→H and degree −1 h with pi=Id and Id−ip=dh+hd. This convention fixes the sign of h.
For commuting raw horizontal and vertical differentials on C^{p,q}, the total differential is δ+(−1)^p∂. Cone(f)ⁿ=Dⁿ⊕Cⁿ⁺¹ has differential (u,v)↦(d_Du+fv,−d_Cv).

theorem.statement: A contraction makes i and p inverse on cohomology. Signed totalization squares to zero, and the stated cone differential squares to zero exactly when f is a cochain map. In particular Cone(Id) is contractible.
theorem.proof: For a cocycle c, the contraction identity gives c−ip(c)=d h(c), hence the classes of c and ip(c) agree. Since pi=Id, the induced maps are inverse. In a bicomplex the two mixed compositions have coefficients (−1)^p and (−1)^{p+1}; they cancel because the raw differentials commute. The remaining squares are zero. Applying the cone differential twice yields ((d_D f−f d_C)v,0), displaying the precise defect. When f=Id, define h(u,v)=(0,u); then dh(u,v)+hd(u,v)=(u,v). This is an explicit contracting homotopy. In finite inner-product complexes, orthogonality gives Cⁿ=im dⁿ⁻¹⊕ker Δ_n⊕im(dⁿ)*, because the orthogonal complement of the two images is exactly the simultaneous kernel of d and d*. Every cohomology class has one harmonic representative, although changing the metric changes that vector.

worked_example.setup: Tensor two complexes Q --Id→ Q concentrated in degrees zero and one, using degree-one coordinates ordered horizontal, vertical.
worked_example.calculation: The total dimensions are (1,2,1). The exact matrices are d⁰=(1,1)ᵀ and d¹=(−1,1). Their product is zero, both maps have rank one, and the Betti vector is (0,0,0). Replacing the second matrix with the unsigned (1,1) produces d¹d⁰=2, so there is no complex over Q. Separately C⁻¹=Qe, C⁰=Qu⊕Qv with de=u contracts onto Qv: set p(u)=0, p(v)=v, i(v)=v, h(u)=e, h(v)=0. Both sides of Id−ip=dh+hd send u to u and v to zero. If de=(1+ε)u, the same certificate survives with h(u)=e/(1+ε) exactly when ε≠−1.
worked_example.meaning: The failure at ε=−1 is a real change of homology: the formerly contractible pair becomes two surviving classes. This makes perturbation a testable algebraic question and identifies the parameter where the reduction stops being valid.

title: Derived products, extension classes and deformation obstructions
central_question: What information survives in Tor, Ext and a tangent complex that an ordinary product or dimension count discards?
synopsis:
Derived constructions retain the effect of relations that ordinary algebra has suppressed. Tensoring a resolution and applying Hom to it produce Tor and Ext; these groups measure failures of exactness rather than furnishing decorative refinements of a product. A particular extension belongs to an Ext group, so the dimension of the ambient group cannot determine whether that extension splits. Likewise a nonzero obstruction space is a location where an obstruction may live, not a proof that every first-order motion fails. The actual class or nonlinear obstruction map must be computed.

This principle unifies three distinct lines of the source corpus. Dual numbers provide an exact module model with nonzero derived tensor groups in all positive degrees. A singular hypersurface supplies an explicit cotangent complex and a failed second-order lift. A differential graded Lie algebra organizes nonlinear compatibility through the Maurer–Cartan equation. These constructions share a mechanism: solve at first order, identify the next defect as a cocycle, and ask whether a correcting term makes it a boundary. Their coefficient rings and degree conventions remain different. A deformation of a scheme, an extension of modules and a flatness problem for an algebra must therefore be connected by an actual functor or comparison theorem before their obstruction groups are identified. The archive’s elliptic self-extension example is especially useful as a boundary: stable objects can have nontrivial self-extensions, whereas an honestly semisimple abelian category has none in positive Ext degree.
definitions: For R=k[ε]/(ε²), let k=R/(ε). A free resolution of k has all positive differentials equal to multiplication by ε.
An element of Ext¹_R(C,A) classifies an extension 0→A→B→C→0 up to the stated equivalence; the zero class is the split extension.
For A=k[x]/(x²) in characteristic zero, the cotangent complex is [A --2x→ A] in degrees −1 and zero. Its derived dual at x=0 is the tangent complex.
In a differential graded Lie algebra, dα+[α,α]/2=0. Writing α=ta+t²b makes the first two equations da=0 and db=−[a,a]/2.

theorem.statement: For dual numbers, Tor_n^R(k,k)≅k and Extⁿ_R(k,k)≅k for every n≥0. The extension 0→k→R→k→0 is nonsplit. At the double point x²=0, a first-order displacement x=at lifts modulo t³ only if a²=0.
theorem.proof: The resolution is exact because the kernel and image of multiplication by ε are both εR. Tensoring it with k makes every differential zero, as does applying Hom_R(−,k), proving the Tor and Ext assertions. An R-linear section of R→k would send 1 to a vector v with εv=0, hence v∈εR, whose quotient is zero; it cannot map back to 1. The direct-sum extension with middle term k⊕k does split although its endpoint Ext group is identical. For the singularity, differentiating x² gives 2x dx. At x=0 this map becomes zero, so the tangent and first obstruction spaces are each k. Direct substitution gives (at+bt²)²=a²t² modulo t³. This computes the actual obstruction map a↦a²; over a field it kills only a=0. In a differential graded Lie algebra, the derivation and Jacobi identities make [a,a]/2 closed when da=0. The next equation is solvable precisely when this cocycle class vanishes, which is a class-level criterion.

worked_example.setup: Use a finite deformation model L¹=Qa⊕Qb, L²=Qc, with da=0, db=c, [a,a]=2c and all other relevant brackets zero.
worked_example.calculation: The first-order term ta is closed. Its quadratic defect is t²c, a nonzero vector that is nevertheless the boundary d(t²b). The correction α=ta−t²b satisfies dα+[α,α]/2=−t²c+t²c=0 exactly. Removing b from the complex makes c a nonzero H² class and prevents the same correction. Thus the raw size of the residual does not decide whether the deformation is obstructed.
worked_example.meaning: The constructive output is a lift or a nonzero quotient class. It specifies exactly which information the derived layer adds, and distinguishes algebraic failure from numerical error in a candidate representative.

title: Filtrations, spectral sequences and information at infinity
central_question: How much of a total object can be recovered from graded pages, truncations and inverse systems?
synopsis:
A filtration is an organized sequence of partial views. Passing to the associated graded records the layers but suppresses how they interact. A spectral sequence progressively restores some of that interaction through differentials. Even after every differential is determined, reconstructing an integral group or ring can require extension and multiplicative data. The source sequence develops this distinction through fibrations, filtered complexes, cohomological shifts and inverse limits. Their common question is not whether the displayed table looks plausible, but which connecting maps remain unknown.

The Hopf fibration and the product S²×S¹ have the same initial Serre page but different transgressions. The finite model below makes the same phenomenon an exact two-coordinate computation. It also exposes a second loss: Z/4 and Z/2⊕Z/2 have the same two graded layers, although only the former has an element of order four. A filtration therefore supports a partial reconstruction interface, with each unknown differential and extension listed as an unresolved input. Perverse shifts and t-structures add a related bookkeeping lesson. The declaration of a heart or a support/cosupport condition changes which cohomological degrees count as an object; it is not recoverable from an unshifted label. Finally an infinite inverse system has genuinely limiting information. The doubling tower of integers has vanishing ordinary inverse limit but a nonzero derived limit; no finite truncation alone certifies that infinite result. These examples justify a hierarchy of outputs: graded dimensions, actual graded groups, filtered groups, rings, and geometric objects.
definitions: Use an increasing filtration F_pC preserved by the differential. A component lowering filtration by r may first appear as the corresponding page differential after earlier components vanish.
An associated graded group is gr_F A=⊕F_pA/F_{p−1}A. It does not include a chosen splitting of the filtration.
For a countable inverse system A₀←A₁←⋯, define Δ:∏A_n→∏A_n by Δ(a)_n=a_n−f_n(a_{n+1}); then lim A=kerΔ and lim¹A=cokerΔ in this setting.

theorem.statement: There exist filtered complexes with identical associated graded differential but different total cohomology. There exist nonisomorphic integral groups with the same associated graded. For the doubling tower Z ←×2 Z ←×2 ⋯, lim=0 and lim¹≅Z₂/Z.
theorem.proof: Let C⁰=Qv and C¹=Qw with v in filtration one and w in filtration zero. Both d=0 and dv=w induce zero on each same-filtration quotient, so their initial graded complexes agree. For dv=w the next filtration-dropping differential is an isomorphism and the total is acyclic; for d=0 both classes survive. For the extension example filter Z/4 by 0⊂2Z/4⊂Z/4 and filter (Z/2)² by one coordinate; each graded layer is Z/2, but their exponents differ. For the inverse limit, a compatible sequence satisfies a₀=2ⁿa_n for all n, hence a₀=0 and all a_n=0. Define S(b)=Σ2ⁿb_n in Z₂, convergent in the 2-adic topology. If b=Δ(a), partial sums telescope to a₀−2^{N+1}a_{N+1}, so S(b)=a₀∈Z. Conversely if S(b)=m∈Z, set a_n=(m−Σ_{j<n}2ʲb_j)/2ⁿ. The numerator is divisible by 2ⁿ, so a_n is an integer and a_n−2a_{n+1}=b_n. Binary digits make S onto Z₂. Thus S induces exactly cokerΔ≅Z₂/Z.

worked_example.setup: Compare the two filtered two-term complexes and the two order-four groups just described.
worked_example.calculation: For dv=w the ranks are one and the Betti vector is (0,0); for d=0 they are zero and the Betti vector is (1,1). Yet each associated graded has one generator in its listed bidegree and zero initial differential. In the group comparison, enumerate element orders: Z/4 has orders (1,2,4,4), whereas (Z/2)² has (1,2,2,2). The order-four test detects an extension invisible to the common graded ranks.
worked_example.meaning: A page is useful evidence with a declared reconstruction stage. It becomes a complete answer only after the required differentials, convergence, extensions and products have been supplied.

title: Spaces, chains, torsion and refined homology
central_question: Which features belong to the space, which to its cell structure, and which survive a change of coefficients?
synopsis:
The topological material repeatedly becomes more informative after the underlying space is specified. A triangle can mean three vertices, its three-edge boundary, or a filled two-simplex. These objects have different chain groups and therefore different homology. A graph drawn on a torus is still a one-dimensional complex until its faces are attached; its cycle rank need not equal the surface’s first Betti number. Polyhedral spheres have the same homology while retaining different symmetry groups. These examples teach how to ask a sharper classification question: first choose the equivalence relation, then ask which invariant can distinguish its classes.

Integer coefficients add a second layer. Rational homology records free rank and erases torsion, so it cannot distinguish every space or quotient. A Smith normal form supplies an exact arithmetic certificate for the torsion, provided row and column operations are unimodular and the relevant quotient is actually the homology group. Reduced homology removes the connected-component contribution in degree zero; intersection homology instead restricts which chains may meet singular strata. The two operations address different questions. The cone on a torus is contractible as an ordinary space, yet lower-middle allowable chains retain two one-dimensional classes because their potential cone fillings meet the forbidden apex. A refinement is useful precisely because its allowed chains and intended invariance are explicit, rather than because the word cohomology was attached to a construction.
definitions: For an oriented finite simplicial complex, ∂[v₀,…,v_k]=Σ(−1)^j[v₀,…,v̂_j,…,v_k]. Its cancellation identity is ∂²=0.
A finite connected graph with V vertices and E edges has free H₁ of rank E−V+1. Attaching faces adds ∂₂ and can kill cycles.
For an integer matrix M with Smith form diag(d₁,…,d_r,0), the cokernel is ⊕Z/d_i⊕Z^{m−r}; units contribute trivial factors.
Intersection homology fixes a stratification and a perversity; allowable chain dimensions at a singular stratum determine which fillings count.

theorem.statement: The triangle boundary has Betti vector (1,1), while the filled triangle has (1,0,0). A cellular model of RP² with one cell in dimensions zero, one and two has ∂₁=0 and ∂₂=2, giving H₁(RP²;Z)=Z/2 and H₂(RP²;Z)=0.
theorem.proof: For the triangle use edges 01,12,02 and boundary columns (−1,1,0), (0,−1,1), (−1,0,1). The matrix has rank two and its kernel is generated by (1,1,−1). With no face this is a nonzero H₁ class. Adding the oriented face 012 gives precisely that vector as ∂₂, so the quotient is zero. In the projective plane, the two-cell attaches to the one-skeleton circle by a degree-two map, hence its cellular boundary is multiplication by two. Its kernel on Z is zero and its cokernel is Z/2. Tensoring the cellular complex with Q makes multiplication by two invertible and kills H₁. Tensoring with F₂ makes that differential zero and produces classes in degrees one and two. This change illustrates why coefficients belong in the question. For the cone on T², allowable one-cycles and their bounding two-chains cannot reach a codimension-three apex at lower-middle perversity. They therefore see the punctured cone, which retracts onto T²; the two degree-one classes survive. A three-chain may reach the apex and fills the link’s two-cycle.

worked_example.setup: Compare a triangle boundary, a filled triangle and the integral cellular projective-plane model.
worked_example.calculation: Exact rational matrix ranks yield (β₀,β₁,β₂)=(1,1,0) and (1,0,0) for the two triangle models. In the projective-plane model the Smith entry is 2, so integral first homology has a generator a with 2a=0. The rational Betti vector is (1,0,0), but the mod-two Betti vector is (1,1,1). Euler characteristics remain consistent: 1−1+1=1 for the projective-plane cell counts and for its mod-two Betti numbers.

title: Persistent topology, interleavings and random birth laws
central_question: How does a topological feature persist through a filtration, and what perturbation or randomness can be certified?
synopsis:
Persistence studies a sequence of spaces together with the maps between them. A barcode records the life of a class, including classes that disappear before the terminal space is reached. This is why the colimit cannot replace a persistence module: a finite bar contributes information during its lifetime even though its eventual image is zero. The archive moves from explicit small filtrations to diagram distances, stability and random birth times. These developments fit one constructive interface: input a legal filtration, compute boundary maps and induced maps on homology, and then declare which comparison theorem applies.

The legal-filtration requirement is essential. A simplex cannot enter before one of its faces. Assigning a dramatic label such as singularity or cavity to a parameter value does not change homology; the chain complex changes when cells or maps change. A metric between persistence diagrams also needs the diagonal. An unmatched point can die by matching to its closest diagonal point, with cost half its lifetime in the usual ℓ∞ convention. Stability then has an exact elementary core: uniformly close functions give mutually shifted sublevel inclusions. Passing to barcode stability adds finiteness or tameness assumptions. Random filtrations supply another useful bridge, because a feature born when all required edges are present has a birth time given by a maximum of random variables. This connects a topological lifetime to an exact order-statistic law without claiming that all random topology reduces to one scalar distribution.
definitions: A filtration K_s⊆K_t for s≤t induces a persistence module H_k(K_s)→H_k(K_t) over a fixed field. A bar [b,d) records a feature born at b and killed at d.
For diagrams with the standard bottleneck distance, match points using ℓ∞ cost and allow arbitrary diagonal points. A point (b,d) has diagonal cost (d−b)/2.
For functions f,g on one space, their sublevel filtrations are F_t={f≤t}, G_t={g≤t}. A uniform bound ||f−g||∞≤ε gives an ε-interleaving by inclusions.

theorem.statement: A triangle whose vertices enter at zero, all edges at one and its face at two has one essential H₀ bar, two H₀ bars [0,1), and one H₁ bar [1,2). For a square whose four edge times are independent uniform variables on [0,1] and whose face enters at one, its H₁ birth B has P(B≤t)=t⁴ and expected lifetime 1/5.
theorem.proof: Before time one the triangle has three components; at one its edge boundary matrix has rank two, merging them and leaving the one-dimensional cycle kernel. At two the face boundary spans that kernel. This proves the bars, including the two simultaneous deaths. For the random square, the unique graph cycle exists exactly when every edge has arrived, so B=max(U₁,U₂,U₃,U₄). Independence gives P(B≤t)=∏P(U_j≤t)=t⁴. The face kills it at one, hence expected lifetime is E(1−B)=∫₀¹P(B≤t)dt=1/5. At a fixed t<1 the first Betti number is its birth indicator, with expectation t⁴. For stability, if f(x)≤t then g(x)≤f(x)+ε≤t+ε, giving F_t⊆G_{t+ε}. The reverse inclusion is identical, and the composites are exactly the ordinary inclusion maps shifted by 2ε. This is the direct interleaving certificate before any diagram theorem is invoked.

worked_example.calculation: Pairing long bar to long bar costs max(1/10,1/5)=1/5. Pairing short bar to short bar costs max(1/5,3/10)=3/10, so the bottleneck is at most 3/10. The point (1,2) has no match of cost below 3/10: its closest listed point has that cost and its diagonal cost is 1/2. Therefore the bottleneck is exactly 3/10. Exhaustive finite matchings including diagonal removals certify this small case.

title: Local-to-global gluing, cellular sheaves and Hodge obstructions
central_question: When can compatible local data be replaced by one global object, and how can the obstruction be calculated exactly?
synopsis:
Gluing is a mapping problem with two distinct outcomes. A sheaf axiom says a compatible family glues uniquely; it does not say every arbitrary family is compatible or that higher cohomology vanishes. The circle examples make this distinction concrete. Two arcs overlap in two components, allowing two discrepancies; local constants can change both discrepancies only by the same amount. Their difference is therefore a one-dimensional global obstruction. This is an exact finite complex with a transparent quotient, not a violation of sheaf gluing.

The same mechanism extends to graph potentials, cellular sheaves and discrete Hodge theory. Edge values are globally integrable exactly when their cycle sums vanish. A spanning tree constructs the potential, while each remaining edge checks one cycle constraint. With matrix or scalar transport, the coefficient system changes the equation itself; the ordinary cycle of the underlying graph need not yield a nonzero sheaf class. A rank-one local system on a circle has cohomology controlled by its total monodromy. Its harmonic representative is then a metric-dependent choice inside a metric-independent quotient. This is especially relevant to source claims based on residuals: a vector with zero Hodge Laplacian residual may be a nonzero harmonic obstruction. Certifying H¹=0 requires a rank or coercivity statement on the entire relevant space, not one successful vector. Transfers between local models similarly need a chain equivalence before they can transport obstruction classes bijectively.
definitions: For a connected oriented graph, D:C⁰→C¹ sends a potential f to edge differences f(head)−f(tail). Gluable edge data are imD; H¹=C¹/imD when no two-cells are present.
For the constant real sheaf on a two-arc circle cover with disconnected overlap, the Čech map is R²→R², (a,b)↦(b−a,b−a).
A rank-one local system on an m-cycle has nonzero transports r_j and differential (δs)_j=s_{j+1}−r_js_j. Its loop multiplier is h=∏r_j.

theorem.statement: On a connected graph, edge data are a potential difference exactly when every oriented cycle period vanishes; the potential is unique up to a constant. For the rank-one circle system, H⁰ and H¹ each have dimension one if h=1 and both vanish if h≠1.
theorem.proof: Necessity of zero periods follows by telescoping potential differences around a closed walk. For sufficiency choose a root and define f(v) by summing edge data along a tree path to v. A zero period on the closed walk formed with any other path proves path independence. Every edge then has the required difference; two solutions differ by a function with zero difference on every edge, hence a constant. For the local system, a global section satisfies s_{j+1}=r_js_j. Once s₀ is chosen all others follow, and closure requires (h−1)s₀=0. Thus the kernel is one-dimensional when h=1 and zero otherwise. The differential is square, so rank-nullity gives the same cokernel dimension. Rescaling the basis at vertices changes individual transports but telescoping shows their product is unchanged. In a higher-dimensional cellular sheaf, face-composition identities must additionally make δ²=0; arbitrary transport matrices alone do not guarantee a complex.

worked_example.setup: Use a three-cycle over Q. Compare transports r=(2,3,1/6) and r=(2,3,1), with δ rows expressing the three stated equations.
worked_example.calculation: The first product is one and (1,2,6) spans the kernel. The differential has rank two and a one-dimensional cokernel. The second product is six, forcing s₀=6s₀ and hence all section coordinates zero; the differential is invertible over Q. For additive triangle data (1,2,−3), total period is zero and f=(0,1,3) glues them. Replacing the last value by −2 gives period one and no potential. These exact checks distinguish coefficient holonomy from the graph’s ordinary cycle rank.
worked_example.meaning: The correct interactive output is a potential or an obstruction certificate, together with the coefficient system and a gauge convention. A residual can supplement this certificate but cannot replace its quotient meaning.

title: Periods, cocycles, winding and characteristic classes
central_question: Which global defects survive changes of local choices, and what makes their values topological?
synopsis:
A cocycle expresses consistency of repeated composition; a coboundary expresses a defect removable by changing local choices. Periods and characteristic classes provide ways to detect what remains. The archive contains several versions: winding of a nonvanishing loop, projective phases of group actions, transition functions of bundles and characteristic-form integrals. They share an invariance mechanism, but their coefficients, degrees and products differ. A useful synthesis keeps the actual equation visible rather than treating every nonzero loop quantity as the same obstruction.

Winding is protected by avoidance of the origin: a continuous nonvanishing loop has an integer degree, and a homotopy through nonvanishing loops preserves it. A curl flux is instead a boundary integral depending continuously on the field; equality for two surfaces with the same boundary is a Stokes statement, not automatic quantization. Group projective phases satisfy a two-cocycle equation because multiplication is associative. Rephasing the operators changes the cocycle by a coboundary, while the commutator phase for a commuting pair is unchanged. Bundle transition functions obey their own triple-overlap identity, and characteristic forms connect curvature to integral topology only for a declared bundle and normalization. The source corpus’s four-torus example makes the latter quantitative: if c₁=n dx₁∧dx₂+m dx₃∧dx₄ on the unit torus, then ∫c₁²=2nm, with the factor two arising from degree-two commutativity. A topological density can have a variation that is entirely a boundary term, so it need not furnish a bulk field equation.
definitions: For a nonvanishing piecewise smooth complex loop γ, winding is (2πi)⁻¹∮γ⁻¹dγ. The integral depends on its homotopy class in the punctured complex plane.
For an abelian group written additively, a normalized multiplier σ satisfies σ(g,h)σ(g+h,k)=σ(h,k)σ(g,h+k). Rephasing by b(g) multiplies σ by b(g)b(h)/b(g+h).
A closed differential form is exact only if it has a global primitive; nonzero integral over a closed cycle certifies nonexactness.

theorem.statement: For G=F₂² and σ((a,b),(c,d))=(−1)^{bc}, σ is a two-cocycle which is not a coboundary. The angular form (−y dx+x dy)/(x²+y²) on the punctured plane is closed but not exact.
theorem.proof: For the cocycle, write k=(e,f). The left exponent is bc+(b+d)e, while the right exponent is de+b(c+e); they agree modulo two. Hence the multiplication is associative. If σ were an abelian coboundary, it would be symmetric in g,h because b(g)b(h)/b(g+h) is symmetric. But for g=(1,0), h=(0,1), σ(g,h)=1 and σ(h,g)=−1, a contradiction. The alternating commutator ratio therefore detects the nontrivial projective class and survives rephasing. For the angular form, differentiation gives zero on the punctured plane. Restrict to the unit circle x=cos t,y=sin t: the form becomes dt and its integral is 2π. Every globally exact form has zero integral on a closed loop by the fundamental theorem, proving nonexactness. This is the same local-to-global pattern as gluing, with a de Rham coefficient model rather than finite incidence coordinates.

worked_example.setup: Enumerate the four elements of F₂² and the sixty-four triples, then evaluate the multiplier and its commutator.
worked_example.calculation: Every triple passes the cocycle identity. The chosen coordinate generators anticommute projectively: their multiplier ratio is −1. In the geometric model γ(t)=e^{ikt} with integer k, γ⁻¹γ′=ik, so the winding is k. Under a homotopy that crosses zero, γ⁻¹ is undefined at the crossing and the certificate ceases to apply. For the unit four-torus with n=2,m=3, the normalized characteristic integral is 2·2·3=12, independently of the chosen connection representing that fixed line-bundle class.
worked_example.meaning: The invariant is the class with its hypotheses and normalization. Local changes of gauge alter representatives, while crossing a singularity, changing coefficients or changing the underlying bundle can alter the class itself.

title: Metrics, curvature, scale and transport geometry
central_question: Which conclusions follow from a declared metric, and which survive a change of scale or representation?
synopsis:
Geometry begins with enough data to measure. A coordinate chart does not select a Riemannian metric, a positive symmetric weight table need not satisfy the triangle inequality, and a Jacobian alone does not determine singular values without input and output inner products. These distinctions let the metric material in the archive be organized by constructive outputs: path length, geodesics, curvature, volume growth and transport distance. The archive’s hyperbolic examples are particularly coherent because the metric is explicit and each claimed phenomenon can be computed from it.

On the upper half-plane with ds²=(dx²+dy²)/y², the connection, vertical unit-speed geodesics and curvature −1 agree with the disk model under the Cayley map. Constant metric rescaling changes distances, volumes, curvature and Laplace spectra in related but distinct ways. This blocks a common confusion between a geometric normalization and a dimensionless threshold. Hyperbolic volume growth gives another exact boundary: local Euclidean behavior does not imply a global doubling bound. Discrete Ollivier curvature introduces still another metric construction, comparing probability distributions by optimal transport. Its value depends on the measure convention as well as the graph, and it cannot certify unrelated computational hardness. Prefix ultrametrics supply a complementary geometry: distance is controlled by the first differing digit, while a many-to-one real coding map can erase prefix information through carries. The best synthesis therefore treats metrics as inputs whose consequences can be tested, rather than as labels attached to algebraic expressions.
definitions: A Riemannian metric g assigns positive inner products to tangent spaces; its path distance is the infimum of lengths of curves joining two points.
For a constant c>0, scaling g to c²g multiplies lengths by c, n-dimensional volume by cⁿ, sectional curvature by c⁻² and the scalar Laplacian by c⁻².
For graph measures m_x and m_y, Ollivier curvature on an edge is κ(x,y)=1−W₁(m_x,m_y)/d(x,y), with the measure convention declared.
On b-ary sequences, d(x,y)=a^{N(x,y)} for 0<a<1 and first-difference index N gives an ultrametric, since common prefixes concatenate by a minimum rule.

theorem.statement: The metric g=(dx²+dy²)/y² has Gaussian curvature −1 and vertical unit-speed geodesics y=y₀eᵗ. Hyperbolic three-space has ball volume V₃(R)=π(sinh 2R−2R), and consequently V₃(2R)/V₃(R) is unbounded. For nonlazy uniform-neighbor measures, K₂ has edge curvature zero and K₃ has curvature 1/2.
theorem.proof: For the conformal plane metric e^{2u}(dx²+dy²), K=−e^{−2u}Δu. Here u=−log y, so Δu=1/y² and K=−1. A vertical path y=y₀eᵗ has speed |y′|/y=1 and satisfies the geodesic equation from Γʸ_yy=−1/y. In H³ the sphere area is 4πsinh²r. Integrating from zero to R gives π(sinh2R−2R). Its exponential leading term is (π/2)e^{2R}, so doubling the radius produces an unbounded ratio. For K₂, each nonlazy neighbor distribution is a point mass at the opposite endpoint, so W₁=1 and κ=0. For K₃, the neighbor measures share mass 1/2 at the third vertex; only the other mass 1/2 must move distance one, giving W₁=1/2. A transport plan attains that cost, and the mass discrepancy at one endpoint gives the matching lower bound.

Under 9g, the old unit vertical geodesic has speed three in the same parameter, and reparametrization by t/3 restores unit speed. Gaussian curvature becomes −1/9. A Laplace eigenvalue or quadratic-form spectral threshold scales by 1/9 as well, whereas a dimensionless ratio formed with the squared length scale can remain unchanged.

title: Hamiltonian, symplectic and contact structures
central_question: How do conservation, reduction and projection follow from a specified geometric form?
synopsis:
Symplectic geometry makes dynamical rules structural: a nondegenerate closed two-form converts the derivative of a Hamiltonian into a vector field. Contact geometry replaces this even-dimensional structure with a maximally nonintegrable hyperplane distribution in odd dimension. The archive’s examples become coherent when these forms are written before their consequences. Hamiltonian conservation follows from antisymmetry, a Casimir is a much stronger object, and a cyclic coordinate can be removed only after its conjugate momentum is fixed. A dimension count for a quotient needs a regular constraint and a free action, not just a formal subtraction.

The oscillator links Hamilton’s equations, Hamilton–Jacobi graphs and Riccati evolution without identifying their coordinate descriptions. Its full phase-space flow is smooth for all times. The generating function for the image of one initial graph fails at a caustic because projection to configuration space ceases to be invertible. The divergence is in the graph representation rather than in the trajectory itself. The quiver-style cotangent quotient supplies an equally concrete reduction: solving a moment-map equation and quotienting a free scaling action produces cotangent coordinates, including their canonical one-form. Contact examples then add a compatible but distinct structure. A Legendrian curve satisfies a tangent condition such as dz−y dx=0; on a thermodynamic equilibrium surface the same contact logic yields a potential identity and a Maxwell relation, provided the stated differentiability and change of variables hold.
definitions: Use ω=Σdq_j∧dp_j and define i_{X_H}ω=dH, giving q̇_j=∂H/∂p_j and ṗ_j=−∂H/∂q_j.
A canonical Casimir has zero Poisson bracket with every differentiable function; nondegeneracy forces it to be constant on a connected domain.
For a symmetry generated by translation of q₂, its momentum is p₂. The reduced space at p₂=μ is the momentum level modulo that translation.

theorem.statement: For H=(p₁²+p₂²)/2+V(q₁), reduction at p₂=μ yields ω_red=dq₁∧dp₁ and H_μ=p₁²/2+V(q₁)+μ²/2. For the scaling action on (z,w)∈Cᵐ⊕(Cᵐ)*, the regular quotient {w(z)=0,z≠0}/C* is T*P^{m−1}.
theorem.proof: On the level p₂=μ every tangent variation has dp₂=0, so the pullback of ω is dq₁∧dp₁. Its kernel is precisely the q₂ translation direction. Quotienting removes that kernel and leaves a nondegenerate form. The restricted H is independent of q₂, so it descends; the projected full equations are exactly Hamilton’s equations of H_μ. In the complex quotient, z selects a line ℓ. The constraint makes w vanish on ℓ, and z⊗w defines an invariant map Cᵐ/ℓ→ℓ, canonically a cotangent vector at ℓ. Conversely a cotangent vector has such a representation after choosing a nonzero z, with different choices exactly the scaling action. The moment-map derivative is surjective on z≠0 by varying w, and the action is free there, giving dimension 2m−2. In a chart z₁=1 with z=(1,u), the constraint gives w=(−up,p) and the canonical one-form w·dz is p du.

At t=π/2 all initial q₀ project to q=0 while their momenta differ, so no single-valued p(q) describes the line. The phase-space map is still the exact symplectic rotation. For α=dz−y dx, γ(t)=(t,t,t²/2) satisfies γ*α=t dt−t dt=0 and is Legendrian.

title: Connections, gauge covariance, curvature and holonomy
central_question: How can local transport and global loop effects be distinguished and checked without confusing flatness with triviality?
synopsis:
A connection supplies a rule for differentiating and transporting sections. Curvature measures its local failure to commute in two independent directions; holonomy measures transport around a loop. They interact, but neither is interchangeable with the other or with the topology of the underlying space. A one-dimensional circle supports no curvature two-form and can still have nontrivial monodromy. On a simply connected surface, a nonflat connection can have loop holonomy arising from curvature even when the bundle is topologically trivial. A nontrivial bundle can additionally obstruct a global gauge potential. These distinctions give the archive’s connection and Berry material a common, precise architecture.

Gauge transformations change coordinates in the fibers. They conjugate loop holonomy at its base point, leaving conjugacy-invariant information such as trace, determinant and eigenvalues unchanged. The ordered product matters for matrices; scalar circulation cannot stand in for a nonabelian calculation. The source’s nilpotent shear example is especially effective because its exponentials terminate and its loop product is an exact polynomial. Berry transport adds a geometric realization: eigenlines form a bundle over a parameter space, and local eigenvector choices are gauge choices. A Chern number requires that declared bundle and a normalized curvature integral; it cannot be recovered from a phase function on an unidentified state space. For the spin-half sphere example the integral is one, proving that no globally smooth potential can represent that curvature on the whole sphere.
definitions: For ∇=d+A on a vector bundle, curvature is F=dA+A∧A and ∇² acts by F. Parallel sections satisfy Fv=0, a necessary condition rather than a general converse.
For edge transport U_j:V_j→V_{j+1}, basis changes h_j act by U_j↦h_{j+1}U_jh_j⁻¹. Ordered loop holonomy is the composite returning to its base fiber.
Flat means F=0. Trivial holonomy means every relevant loop acts as identity. Topological triviality means the underlying bundle has a global trivialization; these are different properties.

theorem.statement: A loop holonomy transforms by conjugation at the base vertex. For X=[[0,1],[0,0]] and Y=[[0,0],[1,0]], the loop (I+xX)(I+yY)(I−xX)(I−yY) equals [[1+xy+x²y²,−x²y],[xy²,1−xy]]. Its mixed quadratic coefficient is [X,Y]=diag(1,−1).
theorem.proof: Compose transformed edge maps in path order. Each interior h_j⁻¹ cancels its neighboring h_j, leaving only h₀Hh₀⁻¹; this proves gauge covariance and explains why entries themselves are not invariant. Since X²=Y²=0, exp(xX)=I+xX and exp(yY)=I+yY exactly. Multiplying the four factors gives the displayed polynomial, whose determinant is one and trace is 2+x²y². Setting x=y=ε yields I+ε²[X,Y] plus explicit cubic and quartic terms. This is the exact algebraic mechanism behind a small plaquette limit; a smooth curvature interpretation additionally needs specified base directions, derivative terms and a transport sign convention. On a circle A=iα dθ is flat by dimension, but with parallel transport defined by s′+iαs=0 its holonomy is exp(−2πiα), nontrivial for noninteger α. Thus flatness alone does not force global trivial monodromy.

worked_example.setup: Take x=y=1 in the shear loop and a base gauge h=diag(2,1). Compare it with a rank-one flat circle connection.
worked_example.calculation: The shear holonomy is H=[[3,−1],[1,0]], with determinant one and trace three. Conjugation gives hHh⁻¹=[[3,−2],[1/2,0]], retaining both invariants. For α=1/2 the flat circle holonomy is −1. As a separate curved example on R², A=ix dy has F=i dx∧dy. Parallel transport around a positively oriented unit square is exp(−i) in the stated convention by the scalar Stokes theorem, despite the bundle and base being topologically trivial.
worked_example.meaning: These examples give three independent checks: fiber gauge covariance, local curvature and global monodromy. A numerical loop becomes geometric evidence only after these inputs and conventions are declared.

title: Curves, moving frames and geometric variational models
central_question: Which curve geometry is fixed by curvature, and when does a variational principle actually select a shape?
synopsis:
Curves provide a manageable laboratory for separating geometry, coordinates and dynamics. An affine transformation composes by the semidirect rule, while a time-dependent coordinate frame adds velocity and acceleration terms. A Frenet frame follows a curve’s tangent, normal and binormal; its rotation can be written using a Darboux angular-velocity vector. Neither operation by itself is a new physical law. The archive’s most useful curve examples become explicit once the parameter, regularity and objective are fixed: winding requires a nonvanishing loop, spirograph closure requires commensurate frequencies, and a clothoid minimizes one declared curvature-rate energy with endpoint curvatures.

The variational distinction is especially important. Minimizing the squared derivative of curvature under fixed endpoint curvatures selects linear curvature, but prescribing endpoint positions and tangent directions adds integral constraints and changes the admissible problem. A clothoid is therefore an exact solution of a clearly stated functional, not a universal optimal connector. Extrinsic surface geometry makes a parallel point about normalization: if mean curvature is the average of the principal curvatures, a round sphere has Willmore energy 4π at every radius; using their sum changes the scale by four. Surface immersion, embedding and eversion are also different questions. The curve and surface material consequently contributes a practical discipline: identify the geometric object, pick invariant quantities, state the boundary data and only then optimize or classify.
definitions: For a unit-speed regular space curve with nonzero curvature, the Frenet equations are T′=κN, N′=−κT+τB and B′=−τN. Their Darboux vector is Ω=τT+κB.
For a planar unit-speed curve, θ′=κ and γ′=(cosθ,sinθ). A curvature function plus an initial position and tangent determines the curve by integration.
Fix L>0 and endpoint curvatures κ(0)=κ₀, κ(L)=κ₁. The curvature-rate objective is J[κ]=(1/2)∫₀ᴸ(κ′)²ds on absolutely continuous κ with square-integrable derivative.
With averaged mean curvature H=(κ₁+κ₂)/2, the Willmore functional is ∫H²dA. Its normalization must be stated before numerical comparison.

theorem.statement: The unique minimizer of the stated curvature-rate problem is κ(s)=κ₀+(κ₁−κ₀)s/L, with J_min=(κ₁−κ₀)²/(2L). The associated tangent angle is θ₀+κ₀s+(κ₁−κ₀)s²/(2L). A round sphere has averaged-mean-curvature Willmore energy 4π independently of radius.
theorem.proof: Write κ=κ_lin+η with η(0)=η(L)=0. Expanding J gives J[κ]=J[κ_lin]+(κ₁−κ₀)∫η′/L+(1/2)∫(η′)². The cross term vanishes because the endpoint difference of η is zero. The last term is nonnegative, with equality only when η is constant, hence zero. This proves existence and uniqueness without assuming an unproved Euler–Lagrange conclusion. Integrating θ′=κ gives the quadratic phase, and integrating the unit tangent yields Fresnel-type coordinates. For a sphere of radius R, both principal curvatures have magnitude 1/R, so H²=1/R² and area=4πR², giving 4π. The Frenet–Darboux identity follows directly from the oriented orthonormal cross-product relations: Ω×T=κN, Ω×N=−κT+τB and Ω×B=−τN. It describes the same frame rotation rather than an additional dynamical postulate.

worked_example.setup: Set L=2, κ₀=0, κ₁=2 and θ₀=0. Compare linear curvature with κ_a(s)=s+a s(2−s).
worked_example.calculation: The minimizer is κ=s with θ=s²/2 and J=1. Since κ_a′=1+2a−2as, direct integration gives J[κ_a]=1+4a²/3, strictly larger for a≠0. For a moving affine frame y=M(t)x+b(t), differentiation gives ẏ=Mẋ+Ṁx+ḃ and ÿ=Mẍ+2Ṁẋ+M̈x+b̈; the extra terms are coordinate effects determined by the frame. For a two-frequency spirograph with both coefficients nonzero, rational frequency ratio gives a common period, while irrational ratio prevents one by uniqueness of finite exponential sums.
worked_example.meaning: The constructive geometric object comes from integrating declared local data. Optimality, closure and coordinate covariance each have their own explicit conditions, allowing the interactive atlas to vary one assumption at a time.
